tool.name: OAuth, OIDC & JWT
tool.tagline: Delegated authorization, single sign-on and signed tokens for web APIs
tool.description: OAuth 2.0 lets applications obtain limited access to APIs on a user's behalf without seeing their password; OpenID Connect adds a standard identity layer for login and single sign-on; JSON Web Tokens are the signed token format both commonly use. Together they secure almost every modern web, mobile and machine-to-machine API, so understanding the flows and their pitfalls is essential for backend and frontend engineers alike.
tool.version: OAuth 2.0 + RFC 9700 security BCP, OIDC Core 1.0, JWT (RFC 7519)

glossary.def: In security, a string an app presents to prove something — usually that it's allowed in — like a hotel key card.
Letting an app do a limited set of things on your behalf at another service, without giving it your password.
Request for Comments: one of the numbered documents that define internet standards, such as RFC 6749 for OAuth 2.0.
In OAuth, a named permission a token carries, such as orders.read; the API allows only what the scopes cover.
Cancelling a token before it expires, so it stops working.
In OAuth, the user who owns the data an app wants to access.
In OAuth, the service that signs the user in, asks for consent and issues tokens, such as Okta, Auth0 or Google.
In OAuth, the API that holds the data and accepts access tokens.
A variant of base64 that uses - and _ instead of + and /, so encoded data can sit safely in URLs; JWTs use it.
The method used to sign a JWT, named in its header, e.g. HS256 (shared secret) or RS256 and ES256 (key pairs).
One statement inside a JWT's payload, such as sub (who it's about) or exp (when it expires).
A value computed from data and a key that proves who produced the data and that nobody changed it.
A way of signing data with one shared secret that both the signer and the checker know; HS256 in JWTs.
JSON Web Signature: the usual, signed-but-readable form of a JWT.
JSON Web Encryption: a JWT whose contents are encrypted so only the intended receiver can read them.
One of OAuth's recipes for how a client obtains a token, such as the authorization code or client credentials grant.
A short-lived, one-time code the authorization server sends back through the browser, which the client then swaps for tokens.
The authorization server URL where the browser is sent so the user can sign in and approve access.
The authorization server URL a client calls directly to get tokens, for example by swapping an authorization code.
The address in your app that the authorization server sends the browser back to after sign-in; it must be registered in advance.
An OAuth client that can keep a secret, such as an app running on your own server.
An OAuth client that can't keep a secret, like a mobile or single-page app, because its code runs on the user's device.
Messages that pass through the user's browser, such as redirects; their URLs can leak into history and logs.
Direct server-to-server requests that never pass through the browser.
An OAuth add-on where the client proves, when swapping an authorization code, that it is the same client that started the sign-in.
In PKCE, the random secret a client creates per sign-in and reveals only when swapping the code for tokens.
In PKCE, the hash of the code verifier, sent at the start of the sign-in so the server can check the verifier later.
A long-lived token a client sends only to the authorization server to get new access tokens without asking the user again.
A random-looking token that carries no readable data; the API must ask the authorization server what it means.
An API asking the authorization server whether a token is still valid and what it allows.
Regularly replacing a secret or token with a new one, so an old copy stops working.
In OpenID Connect, a signed JWT for the client app saying who the user is and when they signed in.
A random value used once: the client sends it at sign-in and checks it comes back in the ID token, so old tokens can't be replayed.
The service that created a token, named in its iss claim, e.g. https://accounts.google.com.
The OpenID Connect URL that returns a signed-in user's profile details when called with an access token.
A JSON file every OpenID Connect provider publishes at /.well-known/openid-configuration listing its URLs, keys and features.
An OAuth grant where a program gets an access token for itself, with no user involved.
A way for an OAuth client to prove its identity by signing a short JWT with its own private key instead of sending a shared secret.
TLS where the client also presents a certificate, so the server knows exactly which program is connecting.
Letting a program running on a platform (a cloud or Kubernetes) swap the identity token the platform gives it for an access token, with no stored secret.
JSON Web Key Set: the list of public keys an issuer publishes so anyone can check its JWT signatures.
Key id: the JWT header field saying which of the issuer's keys signed the token.
Who a token is meant for, in its aud claim; an API must reject tokens addressed to someone else.
Small differences between servers' clocks; token time checks allow a little leeway for them.
The identity making a request — a user or a program — as the API sees it after checking the token.
An API bug where a caller can read or change someone else's object just by changing its id in the request.
An app installed on a phone or computer, as opposed to a website.
The device's real web browser (or an in-app tab it provides), which the app itself can't spy on.
A web page view built into an app; the app controls it and can read what's typed into it.
Backend for frontend: a small server of your own that handles OAuth for a web app and keeps tokens away from browser JavaScript.
An old, retired OAuth grant that returned tokens directly in the browser's redirect URL.
Issuing a new refresh token every time one is used and cancelling the old one.
Noticing that an already-replaced refresh token was used again — a sign it was stolen — and cancelling the whole token family.
All the refresh and access tokens that descend from one original sign-in.
Asking a signed-in user to prove who they are again, more strongly, before a sensitive action.
OpenID Connect's name for the app that relies on the provider to sign users in.
Signing out where your app clears its own session, then sends the browser to the provider to end its session too.
The provider calling your server directly to say a user signed out elsewhere, so you end their session.
An OAuth grant for TVs and command-line tools: the device shows a code, and the user approves it on their phone or laptop.
Swapping one token for another, for example for a narrower token aimed at a specific downstream API.
A JWT attack where the attacker switches the header's algorithm so a careless library checks the signature the wrong way.
Using a JWT meant for one purpose or service, such as an ID token, where a different kind is expected.
A token tied to a key the client holds, so a stolen copy is useless without that key.
Demonstrating Proof of Possession: the client signs a fresh small JWT for each request, proving it holds the key the token is tied to.
A short hash that identifies a public key or certificate.
Tricking a client that uses several authorization servers into sending a code meant for one to another.
Hiding a real page inside an invisible frame on an attacker's site so the user clicks buttons they can't see, like Approve.
Pushed Authorization Requests: the client sends the sign-in parameters to the server directly first, so they can't be tampered with in the browser.
Financial-grade API: strict OAuth security profiles used by banks and payment providers.

concepts.name: What OAuth solves: roles and delegation
concepts.summary: OAuth 2.0 lets an app use some of your data on another service without your password, using tokens; meet its four roles.
concepts.why: Every "Sign in with Google" button, API integration and mobile app's server builds on this model.
concepts.body:
Imagine a printing app that wants to read your photos from a cloud photo service. Before OAuth, the app would ask for your photo-service password and store it: full access to everything, forever, and the only way to stop it was changing your password.

**OAuth 2.0** replaces that with **delegated authorization**: you let the app do a limited set of things on your behalf. It's defined in RFC 6749; **RFCs** are the numbered documents that define internet standards.

Instead of your password, the app gets an access token. A **token** here is a string the app sends with each request to prove it's allowed in, like a hotel key card. It grants only specific permissions, called **scopes** (say, "read photos" but not "delete photos"), for a limited time, and it can be cancelled (**revoked**) without touching your password.

The four roles:

- **Resource owner**: the user who owns the data.
- **Client**: the application wanting access — a website, a phone app, a command-line tool, or another program on a server.
- **Authorization server (AS)**: shows the login page, asks the user for consent and issues tokens (Okta, Auth0, Microsoft Entra ID, Keycloak, Google...).
- **Resource server (RS)**: the API that holds the data and accepts access tokens.

The user only ever types their password into the authorization server's own page, never into the client app.

OAuth is about **authorization** — deciding what an app may do ("this app may read my photos") — not authentication, proving who someone is ("this is Ann"). An access token is meant for the API; the client should treat it like a sealed envelope it never opens. Using plain OAuth to sign people in caused many security holes, which is why **OpenID Connect** (OIDC) adds a standard sign-in layer on top, covered later.

OAuth 2.0 is a family of standards, not one document. Today's security advice is RFC 9700 (OAuth 2.0 Security Best Current Practice, 2025), and the OAuth 2.1 draft gathers it in one place: the authorization code flow with PKCE for everyone, and two older ways of getting tokens (the implicit and password grants) dropped. Later lessons explain each.
takeaways: OAuth gives apps limited, revocable access through tokens instead of passwords
Roles: resource owner, client, authorization server, resource server
OAuth is authorization; OpenID Connect adds sign-in (authentication)
RFC 9700 and OAuth 2.1 describe today's best practice
pitfalls: Treating an OAuth access token as proof of who the user is.

quiz.explain: The authorization server checks who the user is, records their consent and issues tokens.

quiz.q: Why is the password grant (the client app collects the user's password) discouraged?
options: The app sees the user's password, and extra login checks like phone codes can't work
quiz.explain: The whole point of OAuth is that client apps never see the user's password.

concepts.name: JWT structure and claims
concepts.summary: Read a JSON Web Token: three encoded parts — header, claims, and a signature that proves who made it, without hiding anything.
concepts.why: JWTs carry identity and access information in most modern sign-ins and APIs.
concepts.body:
A **JSON Web Token (JWT)** is a small, signed piece of JSON that one system hands to another, like a stamped visitor badge. In security, a string like this that proves something about whoever presents it is called a **token**. A JWT is text in three parts joined by dots: `header.payload.signature`.

Each part is **base64url**-encoded: written using only letters, digits, `-` and `_`, so it travels safely inside URLs and HTTP headers. Encoding is not hiding: anyone can turn it back into JSON.

- The **header** says how the token was signed (the **signing algorithm**, such as `RS256`) and usually which key: `{"alg":"RS256","kid":"2025-10"}`.
- The **payload** is the content: a JSON object whose entries are called **claims**.
- The **signature** is a value computed from `header.payload` and a key. Only someone holding the key could produce it, and changing even one character of the token makes it stop matching.

There are two kinds of keys. With **HMAC** (`HS256`), one shared secret both signs and checks. With a key pair (`RS256`, `ES256`, `EdDSA`), a private key that only the issuer keeps does the signing, and the matching public key, which anyone may have, does the checking.

Registered claims you will see everywhere:

- `iss` issuer (who made the token), `sub` subject (a stable id for the user or app it's about), `aud` audience (who the token is meant for).
- `exp` expiry, `iat` issued-at, `nbf` not-before, all counted in **seconds** since 1 January 1970.
- `jti` a unique token id, useful for spotting a token used twice and for lists of cancelled tokens.

Signed JWTs (JWS) are **not encrypted**: nothing is scrambled. Anyone holding the token can decode the payload and read it, so never put secrets or sensitive personal data inside. Encrypted JWTs (JWE) exist but are less common.

Decoding is not verifying. A token's contents mean nothing until you have checked the signature with a trusted key and checked `iss`, `aud` and `exp`; a later lesson shows how. When troubleshooting, decode tokens on your own machine rather than pasting real tokens into websites.
takeaways: header.payload.signature, each part base64url-encoded
Key claims: iss, sub, aud, exp, iat, nbf, jti
Signed is not encrypted: never put secrets in the payload
Times are in seconds, not milliseconds

quiz.q: What does a valid JWS signature guarantee?
options: The user is still logged in
The token has not been used before
The token was issued by the key holder and not modified
quiz.explain: A signature proves who made the token and that it wasn't changed; it says nothing about secrecy, whether the user is still signed in, or reuse.

concepts.name: Authorization code flow
concepts.summary: Walk through the authorization code flow: send the user to sign in, get a one-time code back, and swap it for tokens.
concepts.why: It is the flow almost every interactive app should use.
concepts.body:
OAuth defines several **grant types**: recipes for how a client gets a token. The **authorization code grant** is the default for any app with a user. It talks to two of the authorization server's URLs; each URL of an API that does one job is called an **endpoint**.

- The client **redirects** the browser (sends it on to another URL) to the AS's **authorization endpoint** with `response_type=code`, its `client_id`, a pre-registered `redirect_uri` (where to come back to), the requested `scope` and a random `state` value.
- The user signs in at the AS and approves the requested access.
- The AS redirects back to `redirect_uri?code=...&state=...`. This **authorization code** is short-lived (often under a minute) and works only once.
- The client checks that `state` matches what it stored, then POSTs the code to the **token endpoint** straight from its server, not through the browser. A **confidential client** — one that can keep a secret, like a server-side app — also proves its own identity here.
- The AS replies with JSON: an `access_token`, `token_type` (`Bearer`), `expires_in`, often a `refresh_token` (for getting new access tokens; covered later), and with OpenID Connect an `id_token`.

Why two steps? Browser redirects form the **front channel**: their URLs end up in browser history, extensions and server logs. The tokens travel only on the **back channel**, the direct server-to-server request.

The `state` value defends against **CSRF** (cross-site request forgery): an attacker's site can't trick your app into accepting the attacker's code, because the attacker can't guess your random `state`.

Redirect URIs (URI is the general name for addresses such as URLs) must be registered in advance and matched exactly by the AS, so codes can't be sent to an attacker's site.

Every client, including single-page apps (websites that run mostly as JavaScript in the browser) and mobile apps, should also use **PKCE** with this flow; that's the next lesson.
concepts.code:
# 1. Browser is redirected to the authorization endpoint
https://auth.example.com/authorize?response_type=code
  &client_id=web-app
  &redirect_uri=https%3A%2F%2Fapp.example.com%2Fcallback
  &scope=openid%20profile%20orders.read
  &state=af0ifjsldkj
  &code_challenge=E9Melhoa2OwvFrEMTJguCHaoeK1t8URWbuGJSstw-cM
  &code_challenge_method=S256

# 2. After login/consent the AS redirects back:
# https://app.example.com/callback?code=SplxlOBeZQQYbYS6WxSbIA&state=af0ifjsldkj

# 3. Back channel: exchange the code for tokens
curl -s https://auth.example.com/token \
  -u "web-app:$CLIENT_SECRET" \
  -d grant_type=authorization_code \
  -d code=SplxlOBeZQQYbYS6WxSbIA \
  -d redirect_uri=https://app.example.com/callback \
  -d code_verifier=dBjftJeZ4CVP-mB92K27uhbUJU1p1r_wW1gFWFOEjXk
# {"access_token":"...","token_type":"Bearer","expires_in":3600,"refresh_token":"..."}
takeaways: The front channel returns a short-lived code; the back channel swaps it for tokens
`state` must come back unchanged and match, to block CSRF
Redirect URIs are registered in advance and matched exactly
Use PKCE with every authorization code flow
pitfalls: Skipping the `state` check on the callback, which lets an attacker sign the victim into the attacker's account (login CSRF).

quiz.q: Why are tokens not returned directly in the browser redirect?
options: The front channel ends up in browser history, logs and extensions
Tokens are too long for URLs
quiz.explain: Returning only a short-lived code keeps the tokens on the direct back channel.

concepts.name: PKCE
concepts.summary: Tie the authorization code to the app that started the flow, using a secret code verifier and its hashed code challenge.
concepts.why: PKCE stops stolen authorization codes from being swapped for tokens, and is required for every client today.
concepts.body:
**PKCE** (Proof Key for Code Exchange, RFC 7636, pronounced "pixy") protects the authorization code. If an attacker intercepts the code — through a malicious app registered for the same custom link type, a leaked log file, or a **proxy** (a server in the middle that relays traffic) — they could otherwise swap it for tokens.

How it works:

- Before redirecting, the client generates a random **code verifier**: 43 to 128 unguessable random characters.
- It sends a **code challenge** in the authorize request: `BASE64URL(SHA256(verifier))` with `code_challenge_method=S256`.
- The AS stores the challenge with the code.
- At the token endpoint the client sends the original `code_verifier`; the AS hashes it and compares the result with the stored challenge.

A thief who has the code but not the verifier cannot exchange it. The verifier never leaves the client until the back-channel token request.

PKCE was invented for **public clients**: mobile and single-page apps, which can't keep a secret because anything shipped to a device can be dug out. RFC 9700 now recommends it for **all** clients, including confidential server-side apps, because it also stops an attacker slipping a stolen code into someone else's sign-in. Always use `S256`; the `plain` method exists only for old clients that can't compute a hash.

Store the verifier for each sign-in attempt next to `state` (and the OpenID Connect `nonce`, covered later). On a server, keep it in the user's **session**: the server's memory of one visitor, linked to them by a cookie. In a browser app, keep it in a JavaScript variable.
takeaways: Challenge = BASE64URL(SHA256(verifier)), method S256
A stolen code is useless without the verifier
Use PKCE for every client, public or confidential
pitfalls: Reusing one verifier across sign-ins, or storing it where other sites can read it.

quiz.q: What does the client send at the token endpoint to prove it started the flow?
quiz.explain: The AS hashes the verifier and compares it with the challenge stored with the code.

concepts.name: Access tokens, refresh tokens and scopes
concepts.summary: Send short-lived access tokens with scopes on API calls, and use refresh tokens to get new ones without bothering the user.
concepts.why: Token lifetimes and scopes are the main levers for limiting damage when something leaks.
concepts.body:
An **access token** is presented to the API in the `Authorization: Bearer <token>` header. It is a **bearer** token: whoever holds it can use it, like cash. Hence:

- Keep access tokens **short-lived** (minutes to an hour; `expires_in` tells you).
- Send them only over TLS, never in URLs.
- Request the minimum **scopes** (`orders.read`, not `admin`). Scopes are strings defined by the API; the AS may grant fewer than requested, and the `scope` value in the token response says what you got.

Access tokens come in two formats. **JWT access tokens** (signed JSON tokens, defined for this use in RFC 9068) can be checked by the API on its own. **Opaque tokens** are random strings that mean nothing by themselves; the API asks the AS about each one, which is called **introspection** (RFC 7662). Clients should treat both as opaque and never parse them: the format is a contract between AS and API.

A **refresh token** is a long-lived secret sent only to the AS's token endpoint (`grant_type=refresh_token`) to obtain a new access token. It lets apps keep working without re-prompting the user, while API-facing tokens stay short-lived.

Refresh tokens are high-value: store them on your server or in the phone's secure storage (Keychain or Keystore), and expect the AS to replace them with a new one on each use (**rotation**). The `offline_access` scope (in OIDC) asks for one explicitly.
concepts.code:
# Call an API with a bearer access token
curl -s https://api.example.com/orders \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $ACCESS_TOKEN"
# 401 + WWW-Authenticate: Bearer error="invalid_token" when it has expired

# Refresh it (confidential client authenticates with its secret)
curl -s https://auth.example.com/token \
  -u "web-app:$CLIENT_SECRET" \
  -d grant_type=refresh_token \
  -d refresh_token="$REFRESH_TOKEN"
# {"access_token":"<new>","token_type":"Bearer","expires_in":900,
#  "refresh_token":"<rotated>","scope":"orders.read"}
takeaways: Bearer tokens work for whoever holds them: short lifetimes, TLS only
Request the minimum scopes; check the granted `scope`
Clients treat access tokens as opaque
Refresh tokens go only to the token endpoint
pitfalls: Putting access tokens in URLs, where they end up in server logs and in the Referer header browsers send to other sites.

quiz.q: Which party should parse and validate the contents of an access token?
quiz.explain: Access tokens are meant for the API; clients must treat them as opaque.

concepts.name: OpenID Connect: ID tokens and login
concepts.summary: Add the openid scope to get an ID token that tells the client who logged in, plus the userinfo endpoint for profile data.
concepts.why: OIDC is the standard behind "Sign in with..." buttons and company-wide single sign-on (one sign-in for many apps).
concepts.body:
**OpenID Connect (OIDC)** is a thin identity layer on top of OAuth 2.0. Add `scope=openid` to an authorization code request and the token response also contains an **ID token**: a signed JWT, addressed to the **client**, stating who the user is and how they proved it.

Important ID token claims:

- `iss` (the provider), `sub` (stable, unique user id within that issuer), `aud` (your `client_id`).
- `exp`, `iat`, and `auth_time` (when the user actually authenticated).
- `nonce`: the random value your client sent in the authorize request; it must match, to stop replayed ID tokens.
- Optional profile claims like `email`, `email_verified`, `name`, depending on scopes (`profile`, `email`).

Identify users by the pair **(`iss`, `sub`)**, never by email: emails change and can be reused, and some providers do not verify them.

The **userinfo endpoint** returns profile claims when called with the access token. Providers publish everything else (endpoints, supported signing algorithms, signing keys) in a **discovery document** at `/.well-known/openid-configuration`.

Keep the token roles straight: the **ID token** is for the client, to start a signed-in session, and is never sent to APIs; the **access token** is for APIs. After checking the ID token, most server-side apps start their own session (the server's memory of the signed-in user, linked by a cookie) and throw the ID token away, keeping it only as `id_token_hint` for signing out later.
takeaways: `scope=openid` adds a signed ID token for the client
Identify users by (iss, sub), not by email
Check `aud` = your client_id and `nonce` = what you sent
ID token for the client, access token for APIs
pitfalls: Sending the ID token to your API as if it were an access token.

quiz.q: Which value should be your database key for an OIDC user?
quiz.explain: `sub` is unique and stable only within its issuer, so combine it with `iss`.

concepts.name: Client credentials for services
concepts.summary: Let a server program get its own access token with the client credentials grant, with no user involved.
concepts.why: Machine-to-machine calls between services, jobs and partners use this grant.
concepts.body:
When no user is involved — a nightly job calling a billing API, one small service calling another — the client acts on its **own** behalf. The **client credentials grant** is a single back-channel request:

`POST /token` with `grant_type=client_credentials`, the requested `scope`, and the client's proof of identity.

There is no refresh token: when the access token expires, the service simply asks for a new one. Keep (cache) it until shortly before `expires_in` runs out instead of fetching one per request; many authorization servers put a **rate limit** (a cap on requests per minute) on the token endpoint.

How the client proves its identity matters. The simple options rely on a shared secret:

- `client_secret_basic` (HTTP Basic with the client id and secret) or `client_secret_post`. Keep the secret in a **secrets manager** (a locked vault service for passwords and keys), hand it to the program as an environment variable, and replace it regularly.

Stronger options remove the shared secret:

- `private_key_jwt`: the client signs a short-lived JWT with its own private key; the AS knows only the public key, so there's no shared secret to leak.
- **mTLS client authentication** (RFC 8705): the client proves itself with its own TLS certificate (mutual TLS).
- On cloud platforms and Kubernetes, **workload identity federation** lets a service trade a token its platform issued to it for an access token, so it holds no long-lived secret at all.

The resulting token's `sub` is the client itself, so APIs decide based on the client's scopes or roles rather than a user's.
takeaways: Client credentials = the service acting as itself, no user
No refresh token: cache the access token until near expiry
Prefer private_key_jwt, mTLS or workload identity to shared secrets
pitfalls: Requesting a new token on every API call and hitting token endpoint rate limits.

quiz.q: Why does the client credentials grant not return a refresh token?
options: The client can simply request a new token with its own credentials
quiz.explain: There is no user to re-prompt, so the client just repeats the grant.

concepts.name: Validating JWTs with JWKS
concepts.summary: Check a JWT's signature against the issuer's published keys (JWKS), fix the allowed algorithms, and check iss, aud, exp and typ.
concepts.why: Every API that accepts JWT access tokens must check them correctly; mistakes here are serious security holes.
concepts.body:
To trust a JWT, a resource server must do all of these, ideally with a well-maintained library such as `jose` (Node), PyJWT, or the one built into your web framework:

- **Fetch the issuer's public keys** from its **JWKS** endpoint (a JSON Web Key Set: the list of its current public keys, at `jwks_uri` in the discovery document). Cache them, and pick the key matching the token's `kid` (key id). Fetch again when you see an unknown `kid`, because keys are replaced over time, but limit how often.
- **Fix the list of signing algorithms** you accept (e.g. only `RS256` or `ES256`). Never let the token's header decide.
- Verify the **signature**.
- Check `iss` equals the expected issuer exactly, and `aud` contains your API's identifier. Without the audience check, a token issued for another API from the same AS would work against yours.
- Check `exp` and `nbf` allowing for small clock differences between servers (**clock skew**, 30 to 60 seconds).
- For access tokens, check `typ` is `at+jwt` (RFC 9068) when the AS sets it, so ID tokens cannot be replayed as access tokens.

Only after all checks pass, read `sub`, `scope` and other claims. Reject with `401` and a `WWW-Authenticate: Bearer error="invalid_token"` header when validation fails.

Local JWT validation is fast but cannot see revocation until the token expires; that is the reason access tokens are short-lived. If you need immediate revocation, use opaque tokens with introspection.
takeaways: Get keys from the issuer's JWKS by `kid`; handle key changes
Fix the accepted algorithms; never trust the header's `alg`
Always check iss, aud, exp (and typ for access tokens)
JWTs stay valid until exp: keep them short-lived
pitfalls: Skipping the audience check, so tokens minted for another API are accepted by yours.

quiz.q: A valid token from your AS was issued for `aud: billing-api`. Your orders API accepts it. What check is missing?
quiz.explain: The audience check ensures a token is meant for this specific API.

concepts.name: Protecting an API: scopes and claims
concepts.summary: Turn checked tokens into access decisions with scopes, roles and ownership checks in your API's request handling.
concepts.why: A valid token only says who is calling; your API still has to decide what they may do.
concepts.body:
After validation, the API holds trustworthy claims. Authorization happens in layers:

- **Authentication middleware** (code that runs before every route handler) checks the token once per request and attaches the caller's identity, the **principal** (`sub`, client id, scopes, roles), to the request.
- **Coarse checks per route**: does the token carry the scope this operation needs? `GET /orders` needs `orders.read`, `POST /orders` needs `orders.write`. Return **403** with `error="insufficient_scope"` when the token is valid but lacks a scope, and **401** when the token is missing or invalid.
- **Fine-grained checks per resource**: scopes say what the *client* may do on the user's behalf, not what the *user* may do. The API must still check that order 123 belongs to `sub` or that the user's role allows the action. Skipping this causes **broken object-level authorization** (BOLA), the top API weakness in the OWASP API Security Top 10 list.

Practical guidance:

- Keep scopes coarse and stable; model detailed permissions in your own database or a policy engine, not as hundreds of scopes.
- Distinguish user tokens from service tokens (client credentials have no user `sub` in the usual sense).
- Log the `sub`, client id and decision for audits, never the token itself.
takeaways: 401 = no or invalid token; 403 = valid token, not allowed
Scopes limit the client; resource checks limit the user
Always verify the caller owns or may access the specific object
pitfalls: Trusting scopes alone and letting any user with `orders.read` read everyone's orders.

quiz.q: A token is valid but lacks the `orders.write` scope. Which status should the API return?
quiz.explain: The caller is authenticated but not permitted: 403 with insufficient_scope.

concepts.name: SPAs, mobile apps and the BFF pattern
concepts.summary: Choose where tokens live for public clients: native apps use the system browser, and single-page apps use a backend-for-frontend.
concepts.why: Most token theft happens in browsers; the client architecture decides how exposed tokens are.
concepts.body:
**Confidential clients** (server-side apps) can keep a secret. **Public clients** (SPAs, mobile and desktop apps) cannot: anything shipped to a device can be extracted. Both use the authorization code flow with PKCE, but token handling differs.

**Native apps** (RFC 8252): open the login page in the **system browser** or an in-app browser tab (ASWebAuthenticationSession, Custom Tabs), never an embedded **WebView** (a browser view built into the app itself, whose contents the app could read, password included). Receive the redirect via claimed HTTPS links (Universal/App Links) or a private-use URI scheme, and store refresh tokens in the Keychain or Keystore.

**Single-page apps** are the hardest case. Any token readable by JavaScript can be stolen by an XSS bug or a compromised dependency. Options, from most to least secure:

- **Backend for frontend (BFF)**: a small server of your own performs the OAuth flow as a confidential client, keeps tokens server-side, and gives the browser an `HttpOnly`, `Secure`, `SameSite` session cookie. API calls go through the BFF. This is the current recommendation for sensitive apps.
- **Token-mediating backend**: the backend gets tokens and hands short-lived access tokens to the SPA.
- **Browser-only**: tokens kept only in JavaScript variables (not `localStorage`), refresh tokens replaced on every use, a strict Content Security Policy (browser rules limiting which scripts may run), and DPoP (later lesson) if available.

The implicit grant (tokens returned directly in the redirect URL) is officially retired (deprecated); don't use it.
concepts.code:
Browser                     BFF (same site)                 Auth server / API
-------                     ---------------                 -----------------
GET /login        ------->  build authorize URL + PKCE
                  <-------  302 to auth server
login + consent   ---------------------------------------->  /authorize
callback ?code=   ------->  POST /token (client secret +      /token
                            code_verifier)          ------->
                  <-------  Set-Cookie: sid=...; HttpOnly;
                            Secure; SameSite=Strict
fetch /api/orders ------->  look up tokens for sid,
  (cookie only)             add Authorization: Bearer ---->  API
                  <-------  JSON                      <----

Tokens never reach JavaScript in the browser.
takeaways: Public clients cannot keep secrets; use code flow + PKCE
Native apps: system browser, never embedded WebViews
SPAs: a BFF keeps tokens server-side behind an HttpOnly cookie
The implicit grant is deprecated
pitfalls: Storing refresh tokens in localStorage, where any XSS can read them.

quiz.q: Why is a backend-for-frontend safer for an SPA than storing tokens in the browser?
options: It removes the need for TLS
Tokens never become readable by JavaScript, so XSS cannot steal them
quiz.explain: With a BFF the browser holds only an HttpOnly session cookie.

concepts.name: Rotation, revocation and introspection
concepts.summary: Rotate refresh tokens with reuse detection, revoke tokens at logout, and introspect opaque tokens when you need live status.
concepts.why: Long-lived credentials need a way to be killed quickly when something goes wrong.
concepts.body:
**Refresh token rotation**: each time a refresh token is used, the AS issues a new one and cancels the old one. If an old refresh token is ever presented again, someone has a copy, so the AS revokes the whole token family and forces re-login. RFC 9700 requires public clients' refresh tokens to be either rotated or sender-constrained.

Handle rotation carefully in clients: two tabs or simultaneous requests refreshing at once can trip reuse detection. Allow only one refresh at a time (share a single in-progress refresh promise); many ASes also allow a short grace period.

**Revocation** (RFC 7009): `POST /revoke` with `token=...` and `token_type_hint=refresh_token`. Call it on logout. Revoking a refresh token usually also revokes the access tokens derived from it, but self-contained JWT access tokens remain usable by APIs until `exp`, which is why access tokens should live minutes, not days.

**Introspection** (RFC 7662): the API POSTs a token to the AS's introspection endpoint and gets `{"active": true, "sub": ..., "scope": ..., "exp": ...}`. It gives live revocation status at the cost of a network call per request (cache results for a few seconds). Use it with opaque tokens or for high-risk operations.

Other kill switches: short session lifetimes at the AS, step-up authentication for sensitive actions, and the Shared Signals framework (CAEP) for real-time session revocation events.
concepts.code:
# Revoke a refresh token at logout (RFC 7009)
curl -s https://auth.example.com/oauth/revoke \
  -u "web-app:$CLIENT_SECRET" \
  -d token="$REFRESH_TOKEN" \
  -d token_type_hint=refresh_token
# HTTP 200 (also for tokens that were already invalid)

# Introspect an opaque access token from the API (RFC 7662)
curl -s https://auth.example.com/oauth/introspect \
  -u "orders-api:$API_SECRET" \
  -d token="$ACCESS_TOKEN"
# {"active":true,"sub":"user-42","client_id":"web-app",
#  "scope":"orders.read","exp":1760003600}
# revoked or expired -> {"active":false}
takeaways: Rotation + reuse detection turns a stolen refresh token into a forced logout
Revoke refresh tokens at logout; JWT access tokens live until exp
Introspection gives live status for opaque tokens
pitfalls: Simultaneous refresh calls in a client triggering reuse detection and signing the user out.

quiz.q: An old, already-rotated refresh token is presented to the AS. What should a rotating AS do?
options: Treat it as theft and revoke the token family
Return a new access token only
quiz.explain: Reuse means two parties hold the token, so the safe response is revoking the whole family.

concepts.name: OIDC discovery, nonce and logout
concepts.summary: Configure clients from the discovery document, validate ID tokens fully, and implement RP-initiated and back-channel logout.
concepts.why: Real SSO integrations need correct session handling, not just a successful login.
concepts.body:
**Discovery**: `GET {issuer}/.well-known/openid-configuration` returns JSON with `authorization_endpoint`, `token_endpoint`, `userinfo_endpoint`, `jwks_uri`, `end_session_endpoint`, and supported scopes, response types and algorithms. Configure clients from it rather than hard-coding URLs, and check that its `issuer` exactly equals the issuer you expect.

**ID token validation** in full: signature via `jwks_uri`, `iss` exact match, `aud` contains your client id (and `azp` if several audiences), `exp`/`iat` sane, `nonce` matches the value stored for this login attempt. Use `auth_time` and the `max_age` request parameter when you need recent authentication; `prompt=login` forces re-authentication and `prompt=none` checks for an existing session silently.

**Logout** in SSO is about several sessions: your app's session, the provider's session, and other apps' sessions.

- **RP-initiated logout**: clear your session, then redirect to `end_session_endpoint` with `id_token_hint` and `post_logout_redirect_uri`.
- **Back-channel logout**: the provider POSTs a signed **logout token** to your registered endpoint when the user logs out elsewhere; validate it and destroy the matching session (by `sid` or `sub`).
- Front-channel logout uses hidden embedded pages (iframes) and increasingly fails now that browsers block cookies from other sites.

Store `state`, `nonce` and the PKCE verifier together per login attempt so sign-ins started in several tabs at once don't overwrite each other.
takeaways: Discovery gives endpoints and jwks_uri; verify its `issuer`
Validate nonce, aud/azp, iss and times on every ID token
Logout spans app and provider sessions: RP-initiated and back-channel
Keep state, nonce and verifier per login attempt
pitfalls: Clearing only the local session, so the next 'Log in' silently signs the user back in via the provider session.

quiz.q: After your app clears its own session, clicking Login immediately logs the user back in without a password. Why?
options: The provider's SSO session is still active
quiz.explain: Ending only the local session leaves the identity provider session alive.

concepts.name: Device flow and token exchange
concepts.summary: Log in on TVs and CLIs with the device authorization grant, and swap tokens between services with token exchange.
concepts.why: Input-constrained devices and service chains need flows beyond the redirect-based one.
concepts.body:
**Device authorization grant** (RFC 8628) serves devices without a usable browser or keyboard: smart TVs, CLIs, IoT devices.

- The device POSTs to the **device authorization endpoint** and gets a `device_code`, a short `user_code`, a `verification_uri` (often also `verification_uri_complete` for QR codes) and a polling `interval`.
- It shows "Visit example.com/device and enter WDJB-MJHT".
- The user completes login and consent on their phone or laptop.
- Meanwhile the device polls the token endpoint with `grant_type=urn:ietf:params:oauth:grant-type:device_code`, receiving `authorization_pending` until the user finishes, and `slow_down` if it polls too fast.

`gh auth login`, `az login --use-device-code` and many streaming apps use it. It is phishable (attackers can send victims a code to approve), so show the client name clearly on the approval screen and keep codes short-lived.

**Token exchange** (RFC 8693) lets a service trade one token for another: `grant_type=urn:ietf:params:oauth:grant-type:token-exchange` with a `subject_token`. Uses include:

- Down-scoping a user's token for a specific downstream API (new `audience`), instead of forwarding the original broad token.
- Delegation chains where the new token records the acting service in an `act` claim.
- Workload identity federation: exchanging a Kubernetes or GitHub Actions OIDC token for a cloud access token.
concepts.code:
# 1. Device asks for codes
curl -s https://auth.example.com/oauth/device/code \
  -d client_id=tv-app -d scope="openid profile"
# {"device_code":"GmRhm...","user_code":"WDJB-MJHT",
#  "verification_uri":"https://example.com/device","expires_in":900,"interval":5}

# 2. Poll every `interval` seconds until the user approves
curl -s https://auth.example.com/oauth/token \
  -d grant_type=urn:ietf:params:oauth:grant-type:device_code \
  -d device_code=GmRhm... -d client_id=tv-app
# {"error":"authorization_pending"}  ...later...  {"access_token":"...", ...}

# Token exchange: get a narrower token for a downstream API
curl -s https://auth.example.com/oauth/token -u "orders-api:$SECRET" \
  -d grant_type=urn:ietf:params:oauth:grant-type:token-exchange \
  -d subject_token="$USER_ACCESS_TOKEN" \
  -d subject_token_type=urn:ietf:params:oauth:token-type:access_token \
  -d audience=https://inventory.example.com
takeaways: Device flow: show a user code, the user approves elsewhere, the device polls
Honour `interval` and `slow_down` when polling
Token exchange swaps a token for one with a narrower audience or delegation
pitfalls: Forwarding a user's broad access token to every downstream service instead of exchanging it.

quiz.q: What does a device receive from the token endpoint while the user has not yet approved?
quiz.explain: It keeps polling at the given interval until approval, denial or expiry.

concepts.name: JWT attacks and hardening
concepts.summary: Recognize alg=none, algorithm confusion, kid and jku injection, and cross-JWT confusion, and apply the JWT best practices (RFC 8725).
concepts.why: Many real breaches came from libraries or code that trusted attacker-controlled JWT headers.
concepts.body:
A JWT header is attacker-controlled input. The classic attacks all exploit code that lets the header decide how to verify:

- **`alg: none`**: an unsigned token accepted by a library that honours the header. Never accept `none`.
- **Algorithm confusion**: a server expects `RS256` but the attacker sends `HS256`, and a naive library uses the RSA **public** key bytes as the HMAC secret. Since the public key is public, the attacker can sign anything. Fix: bind each key to one algorithm and pin allowed algorithms.
- **`kid` injection**: using `kid` to build a file path or database query that loads the key. Treat `kid` only as a lookup key into your own key set.
- **`jku` / `x5u` / embedded `jwk` headers**: fetching keys from a URL the token itself names lets attackers supply their own keys. Ignore these unless restricted to an allow-list.
- **Cross-JWT confusion**: using a token of one kind as another, e.g. an ID token as an access token, or a token for service A at service B. Check `typ`, `aud` and `iss`.
- **Weak HMAC secrets** can be brute-forced offline from a single token; use at least 256 random bits, or asymmetric keys.

RFC 8725 (JWT BCP) summarizes the defences: pin algorithms, validate all relevant claims, use explicit typing (`typ`), and use different keys for different token kinds. Prefer asymmetric signatures when many services verify, so only the issuer can mint tokens.
takeaways: The header is attacker input: pin algorithms, never trust `alg`
Bind each key to one algorithm to stop RS/HS confusion
Ignore jku/x5u/jwk headers; look `kid` up in your own key set
Use `typ` and `aud` to prevent cross-JWT confusion
pitfalls: Writing your own JWT verification instead of using a maintained library with algorithm pinning.

quiz.q: In an algorithm confusion attack, what does the attacker use as the HMAC secret?
quiz.explain: A library that lets the header switch to HS256 may verify with the public key as the HMAC secret.

concepts.name: Sender-constrained tokens: DPoP and mTLS
concepts.summary: Bind access and refresh tokens to a client key with DPoP proofs or mutual TLS so stolen tokens are useless.
concepts.why: Bearer tokens are only as safe as every place they pass through; binding them closes that gap.
concepts.body:
A bearer token works for anyone holding it. **Sender-constrained** tokens additionally require proof of possession of a private key that never leaves the client.

**DPoP** (RFC 9449, Demonstrating Proof of Possession) works at the application layer:

- The client generates a key pair (in the browser via WebCrypto with a non-extractable key, or in secure storage on mobile).
- On each token request and API call it sends a `DPoP` header: a fresh JWT with `typ: dpop+jwt`, its public key in the `jwk` header, and claims `htm` (HTTP method), `htu` (URL), `iat`, a unique `jti`, and for API calls `ath` (hash of the access token).
- The AS binds the token to the key's thumbprint (`cnf.jkt` claim) and uses `token_type: DPoP`; APIs require `Authorization: DPoP <token>` plus a valid proof that matches the method, URL and key.
- Servers may demand a `nonce` (via `DPoP-Nonce`) to limit pre-generated proofs, and must reject replayed `jti` values within the acceptance window.

**mTLS-bound tokens** (RFC 8705) bind the token to the client's TLS certificate (`cnf.x5t#S256`). Strong and transparent for server-to-server traffic, impractical in browsers.

Binding defends against token leakage through logs, proxies, compromised APIs and stolen storage. It does not stop an attacker who can run code inside the client (XSS can still make requests), so it complements, not replaces, the earlier defences. FAPI 2.0 security profiles require sender-constrained tokens.
takeaways: Sender-constrained tokens need proof of a private key
DPoP proofs are per-request JWTs bound to method, URL and token hash
mTLS binding fits server-to-server traffic
Binding stops replay of leaked tokens, not in-client attacks
pitfalls: Accepting DPoP proofs without checking `htm`, `htu`, `jti` replay and the key thumbprint.

quiz.q: What stops a stolen DPoP-bound access token from being used by an attacker?
options: Each request needs a fresh proof signed by the client's private key
quiz.explain: Without the private key, the attacker cannot produce matching DPoP proofs.

concepts.name: OAuth security best practice (RFC 9700)
concepts.summary: Apply the current OAuth threat model: exact redirect matching, PAR, mix-up defence, no implicit or password grants, and OAuth 2.1.
concepts.why: Most OAuth breaches exploit known patterns that RFC 9700 tells you how to close.
concepts.body:
RFC 9700 (OAuth 2.0 Security Best Current Practice, January 2025) is the checklist for any serious OAuth setup. The highlights:

- **Exact redirect URI matching.** No wildcards or prefix matching: open redirectors and lax matching have leaked codes and tokens countless times.
- **PKCE everywhere** with `S256`, and ASes must reject PKCE downgrade attempts.
- **No implicit grant, no resource owner password grant.** Use the authorization code flow.
- **Mix-up attacks**: a client talking to several ASes can be tricked into sending a code to the wrong one. Defend with the `iss` parameter in authorization responses (RFC 9207) or distinct redirect URIs per AS.
- **Sender-constrain or rotate refresh tokens** for public clients; prefer sender-constrained access tokens.
- **Restrict token privileges**: audience-restricted, minimal-scope access tokens.
- Prevent **clickjacking** of authorization pages and **CSRF** with PKCE or `state`.

Beyond the BCP:

- **PAR** (Pushed Authorization Requests, RFC 9126): the client POSTs the authorization parameters to the AS first and gets a `request_uri`, so they cannot be tampered with in the browser and long requests do not hit URL limits.
- **RAR** (Rich Authorization Requests, RFC 9396) expresses detailed permissions like "pay 45 EUR to this account" via `authorization_details`.
- **OAuth 2.1** (draft) folds all of this into one document.
- **FAPI 2.0** profiles combine PAR, PKCE, sender-constrained tokens and strict client authentication for banking-grade APIs.
concepts.code:
# Pushed Authorization Request (RFC 9126): parameters go server-to-server
curl -s https://auth.example.com/oauth/par \
  -u "web-app:$CLIENT_SECRET" \
  -d response_type=code \
  -d client_id=web-app \
  -d redirect_uri=https://app.example.com/callback \
  -d scope="openid payments" \
  -d state=af0ifjsldkj \
  -d code_challenge=E9Melhoa2OwvFrEMTJguCHaoeK1t8URWbuGJSstw-cM \
  -d code_challenge_method=S256
# {"request_uri":"urn:ietf:params:oauth:request_uri:6esc_11ACC5bwc014ltc14eY22c","expires_in":60}

# The browser redirect then only carries client_id and request_uri:
# https://auth.example.com/authorize?client_id=web-app&request_uri=urn:ietf:params:oauth:request_uri:6esc_11ACC5bwc014ltc14eY22c

# Callback with RFC 9207 issuer identification (check iss before redeeming the code):
# https://app.example.com/callback?code=...&state=af0ifjsldkj&iss=https%3A%2F%2Fauth.example.com
takeaways: Exact redirect URI matching, PKCE S256, no implicit or password grants
Defend against mix-up with the `iss` response parameter
PAR moves authorization parameters to the back channel
OAuth 2.1 and FAPI 2.0 package these practices
pitfalls: Allowing wildcard redirect URIs for convenience in production.

quiz.q: What does checking the `iss` parameter on the authorization response defend against?
options: Mix-up attacks between multiple authorization servers
quiz.explain: It tells the client which AS issued the code, so it is not sent to the wrong token endpoint.
